public_rationale: The Decoder reported on June 5, 2024 that Kevin Scott said early looks at next-generation models suggest they could pass PhD qualifying exams, while GPT-4-class models perform like high school students on AP exams (e1). Scott added that this 'probably sounds like a bigger deal than it actually is' (e1). The report does not show him naming GPT-5. 'Blow away PhDs' is Marcus's paraphrase. In August 2025, OpenAI reported that GPT-5 pro scored 88.4% on GPQA without tools (e2). That points to large benchmark gains, but the figure is reported by OpenAI itself. The claim does not say how to measure 'far more modest', and the hint it compares against is hedged and does not name a specific model. So the claim cannot be scored true or false.
limitations: The benchmark figures come from OpenAI and were not independently checked.
Scott's remarks are known only from a news report (e1), not from a primary recording or transcript in the evidence.
The evidence gives no GPT-4 score on the same benchmarks, so it does not measure the size of the improvement directly.
The evidence does not address GPT-5's real-world usefulness compared with GPT-4.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: GPT-5's improvements over GPT-4 were far more modest than Kevin Scott had hinted.

from_speaker: in reality the improvements were far more modest
our_interpretation: Scott's recorded June 2024 remark was that next-generation models 'could pass PhD qualifying exams', compared with GPT-4 matching high schoolers on AP exams. He also said it 'probably sounds like a bigger deal than it actually is'. He did not name GPT-5 in the coverage I read.

'Blow away PhDs' is Marcus's paraphrase. 'Far more modest' has no measure. On benchmarks such as GPQA, GPT-5 scores very high, but whether the real-world gain was 'far more modest' than a hint is a judgment call.
There is no plain, agreed measure for comparing a hint to an outcome, so I treat this as not adjudicable.
criteria.support_condition: Would need an agreed measure showing GPT-5's gains over GPT-4 fell well short of PhD-level performance Scott hinted at; no such agreed measure exists.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Would need an agreed measure showing GPT-5 met or exceeded the PhD-exam level Scott hinted at; benchmark results point that way but do not settle a subjective 'far more modest' judgment.
